recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Pocket Node for iOS: a self-custody CKB light client for iPhone, iPad, and Mac
recent_posts.author: knmo
recent_posts.content_text:
Jnr6:
I would have to strip that device cost out and absorb the hardware myself. I’m also targetting three Apple platforms and a CCC signer the Android app does not have
You’ve already been paid for the Android implementation. That initial work was worth significantly more than porting to Apple platforms is worth. There are several platforms—you say there are three, which I already consider a lot—and what about future device compatibility? Will other types additionally be added at some point? Is there even a need for Apple support, or will it end up being just a handful of people? It seems to me like you’re using a sledgehammer to crack a nut here. And if you’re just starting to buy Apple devices yourself, then you probably don’t have much experience with them yet. Problems or delays are more likely.
You describe how potential dApps can be used equally by CCC signers, and that iCKB is just one prominent example. But even this prominent example has negligible usage. And how much of that negligible usage came from potential Apple users? This was just meant to spark some thought. An Apple user can install Neuron on their desktop or Bitcoin Light on their mobile device. I know that none of these are solutions comparable to PocketNode. But Apple users can certainly use CKB if they want to.
In my opinion, you should at least remove the dApp browser and any CCC-related features from your proposal. The PocketNode wallet could be as functionally and visually similar as possible to the Android version and be available only for the most popular Apple platform—presumably a fairly new one.
Cellora — designing a production indexing and query service for CKB (feedback welcome)
“like likes like”
Don’t you think someone who has already worked extensively with Apple and already possesses the necessary knowledge and devices would be better suited for porting PocketNode?
I’m curious about Hanssen0’s idea for a peer-to-peer application connection.
I have reservations about integrations combining QuantumPurse, Neuron and PocketNode. These are separate projects, even though the developers probably share their knowledge and experience. Post-quantum-secure encryption will also become the default standard for transactions at Nervos in the medium term.

recent_posts.author: Jnr6
recent_posts.content_text:
knmo:
That initial work was worth significantly more than porting to Apple platforms is worth
I created the misunderstanding, when i used the word “Port” in the proposal, that created the idea of everything needed is already implemented and just need to be transfered over. while in reality, what i can transfer over is, the protocol logic(in rust), UI and UX, the DAO math and the sync-mode model; all these are already designed on android and i don’t have to reinvent the wheel, the rest of the work doesn’t exist on Pocket node and i have edited the proposal to indicate that.
knmo:
There are several platforms—you say there are three, which I already consider a lot—and what about future device compatibility?
The “several platform” is another misunderstanding created by my choice of word, there are two codebase, Android and iOS, everything else is under this two platform, if you’re are refering to the Ipad and native Mac OS includeed, that is not a separate codebase, the work from iOS trickles down and the bulk of the work for those two comes from form factor design work and separate QA and review cycle per target, same goes for the android platform too; which add to the work load and i will be removing them.
knmo:
And if you’re just starting to buy Apple devices yourself, then you probably don’t have much experience with them yet. Problems or delays are more likely.
Not using an apple device is a personal choice, I have experienced both and i choose android as my daily driver(it gives me room for tinkering) and i use a macbook for work (testing the mac OS app is easy),owning a device doesn’t mean having building experience, plus you said problems and delay are more likely that statement itself is a guess, also that is what the milestone on the proposal is for, you don’t proceed if previous milestones are not cleared and the code is out in the open, anyone can compile and run it
knmo:
You describe how potential dApps can be used equally by CCC signers, and that iCKB is just one prominent example. But even this prominent example has negligible usage.
I didn’t just come up with this or decided to build this on my own, this conversation has been ongoing for several months, both in my first proposal which i linked earlier. If you look at what is currently being built in the CKB ecosystem, a lot of it is web-based. Pocket Node being able to act as the identity/signing layer gives those applications a way to interact with the wallet without giving them access to the wallet’s internal light client or keys, also this is not about iCKB alone. and the other solution in the apple ecosystem in your own word are solutions not comparable to PocketNode
knmo:
In my opinion, you should at least remove the dApp browser and any CCC-related features from your proposal. The PocketNode wallet could be as functionally and visually similar as possible to the Android version and be available only for the most popular Apple platform—presumably a fairly new one.
your concern here is that PN is swaying away from it original goal.Pocket Node still uses its own internal light client. That light client is not shared with the dApp. The keys stay on the device. A website cannot access either of them. It can only ask Pocket Node for identity or ask the user to sign something, and the user still sees and approves that inside Pocket Node.
So for me the principle is still the same: your node, your keys, no trusted server in the middle.
So I will remove native macOS and iPad support from this proposal, focus the funded Apple implementation on iPhone, and reduce the funding request accordingly.
I’ll update the proposal to reflect that.

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB Builder Lab: Interactive Developer Onboarding Infrastructure for the CKB Ecosystem
recent_posts.author: devnash
recent_posts.content_text:
Week 4 Progress Report: CKB Builder Lab
Hello everyone,
This is the Week 4 progress report for CKB Builder Lab, our Spark Program project focused on interactive developer onboarding for the CKB ecosystem.
Week 4 Milestone
The Week 4 milestone was:
Challenge MVP completed.
The planned tasks were:
implement the challenge framework
add automatic validation
create the first learning challenges
return clear passed or failed results
These tasks have been completed.
What We Implemented
Automatic Challenge Verification
The challenge system is now connected to the simulator engine.
When the learner clicks Simulate, the application:
Builds a draft transaction from the interface.
Sends it to the simulator engine.
Receives the simulation result and validation trace.
Evaluates the result against the active challenge criteria.
Returns automatic passed or failed feedback.
No manual challenge review is required.
Failed submissions preserve the learner’s draft so they can correct the problem and try again.
Initial Challenges
The challenge MVP includes three executable Cell Model challenges:
Create Your First Cell
Verifies Cell creation, positive capacity, lock ownership, and data.
Execute State Transition
Verifies input consumption, witness authorization, and output creation.
Transfer Ownership
Verifies that Alice unlocks the input Cell and creates a Bob-owned output Cell.
Separate Simulation and Learning Validation
The simulator engine determines whether a transaction is technically valid.
The challenge engine separately determines whether the intended learning objective was completed.
For example, Alice can create another Alice-owned output Cell and produce a valid transaction. However, the ownership-transfer challenge still fails because ownership did not change to Bob.
This distinction demonstrates that the challenge system is not simply displaying the simulator’s valid or invalid result.
Sequential Progression
Challenges unlock in order:
Challenge 1 is available immediately.
Challenge 2 unlocks after Challenge 1 passes.
Challenge 3 unlocks after Challenge 2 passes.
Locked challenges cannot be opened early.
Completed challenges remain available for replay.
Progress is displayed as:
0/3
1/3
2/3
3/3
After Challenge 3 passes, the interface displays:
Learning path complete
Criteria, Feedback, and Hints
Each challenge includes:
a learning concept
a practical task
success criteria
completed and failed criteria indicators
progressive hints
automatic feedback
next-challenge navigation
The feedback explains the specific problem, such as:
missing output lock
missing owner witness
input Cell not consumed
output Cell not created
ownership did not change
Browser Progress Persistence
Challenge progress is saved in browser localStorage.
The saved progress contains:
completed challenge IDs
active challenge ID
last update timestamp
After refreshing the page, completed progress is restored.
Stored progress is validated before use:
unknown challenge IDs are removed
duplicates are removed
out-of-order completion is rejected
invalid active challenges fall back to the first unlocked challenge
The interface also includes a reset control that clears saved progress and returns the learner to Challenge 1.
Relationship With Previous Weeks
Week 2: Implemented the simulator engine and transaction validation.
Week 3: Implemented the interactive Cell editor and transaction visualization.
Week 4: Converts the simulator into a structured, automatically verified learning experience.
Tests cover successful and failed challenge submissions, sequential unlocking, progress ordering, saved-progress recovery, missing locks, missing witnesses, and ownership-transfer validation.
Video Evidence
The Week 4 demonstration video shows:
challenge progress reset
locked challenge states
automatic passed and failed results
missing-witness failure
valid transaction with a failed learning objective
successful Alice-to-Bob ownership transfer
complete 3/3 learning path
browser progress persistence

Week 4 is complete.
CKB Builder Lab now has a working challenge MVP with automatic verification, criteria-level feedback, sequential progression, progressive hints, browser-local progress persistence, progress reset, and a final learning-path completion state.
The project is ready for Week 5, which will focus on expanding and refining the beginner lessons, explanations, and onboarding content.

topics.title: Proof of Buy，一种专为Layer1设计的Layer2共识

recent_posts.topic_title: Proof of Buy，一种专为Layer1设计的Layer2共识
recent_posts.author: Lawliet_Chan
recent_posts.content_text:
补，如何解决L2出块间隙比L1短的情况下的出块共识问题
前面我们提及了proof of buy要在出块共识的时候通过 VDF + 支付L1 token的方式来竞选出块权， 但我没有解释一个问题，如何支付L1 token？
我们都知道， L2的出块间隔 跟L1往往不同， 如果L2比L1出块更慢还好， 倘若L2出块比L1更快呢？ 此时，如果矿工支付L1 token来竞选高度为100的L2区块，那么当发起了一笔L1 token的转账之后，L2 的第100个区块已经要出块了，而L1的出块还早，这就导致你这个支付token的交易在L1上还未出块呢， L2已经出块了。 此时L2看不到此时L1 token谁支付的多，它便不知道当前块高的出块权应该给谁。
该问题如果不解决，那么使用proof of buy的L2的出块时长就必然会受制于L1的出块时长。 最终导致L2为求更好的解决方案不得不重回 pos + BFT之类的共识（比如 stacks的poX）
预支付
针对此类问题，proof of buy可启用预支付的方式，即矿工们可以提前一次性 为未来 N个区块 总共支付一笔L1 token。 然后每次L2出块时从中声明出部分额度来表示自己愿意为此次出块所支付的L1 token数量。具体流程如下：
从创始区块开始，矿工先在L1上隐私支付一笔token (我们假设其token数量是一个密文承诺，记作 A) 给proof of buy指定的地址。这之后， 每次L2出块的时候， 矿工在本地生成VDF Output的同时，也需要声明自己要为该区块支付的一笔L1 token数量，记作 a_n（a_n为明文数字，n表示块高。不需要在L2上真正支付，因为之前已经在L1上支付过了） 并生成一个zk proof，证明 a_0 + a_1 + … + a_n <= A， 此处表示自己已为该L2区块预支付过token了且金额足以支付从0到n的这些区块。
其他L2矿工拿到 (VDF_output，a_n, zk_proof) 之后， 根据L1上的A来验证 zk_proof，证明通过之后，将 VDF_output 和 a_n 代入计算中 来算出值 以得出该高度谁最终赢得出块权。

该问题如果不解决，那么使用proof of buy的L2的出块时长就必然会受制于L1的出块时长。 最终导致L2为求更好的解决方案不得不重回 pos + BFT之类的共识（比如 stacks的poX）

预支付

针对此类问题，proof of buy可启用预支付的方式，即矿工们可以提前一次性 为未来 N个区块 总共支付一笔L1 token。 然后每次L2出块时从中声明出部分额度来表示自己愿意为此次出块所支付的L1 token数量。具体流程如下：

从创始区块开始，矿工先在L1上隐私支付一笔token (我们假设其token数量是一个密文承诺，记作 A) 给proof of buy指定的地址。这之后， 每次L2出块的时候， 矿工在本地生成VDF Output的同时，也需要声明自己要为该区块支付的一笔L1 token数量，记作 a_n（a_n为明文数字，n表示块高。不需要在L2上真正支付，因为之前已经在L1上支付过了） 并生成一个zk proof，证明 a_0 + a_1 + … + a_n <= A， 此处表示自己已为该L2区块预支付过token了且金额足以支付从0到n的这些区块。

其他L2矿工拿到 (VDF_output，a_n, zk_proof) 之后， 根据L1上的A来验证 zk_proof，证明通过之后，将 VDF_output 和 a_n 代入计算中 来算出值 以得出该高度谁最终赢得出块权。

Thank you for providing this overview.
I noticed that the people commonly known as the co-founders of Nervos/CKB—Jan Xie, Terry Tai, Kevin Wang, Daniel Lv and Cipher Wang—are not listed among the leads of CKBA’s execution teams.
I understand that this post may only list the current execution-team leads, rather than the Board, Contributing Members, advisers, employees, or individual contributors. Therefore, their absence from this list does not necessarily mean that they have left CKBA or the wider CKB ecosystem.
Could CKBA please clarify:
Do any of the co-founders currently hold a formal role in CKBA—for example as a Board member, Contributing Member, adviser, employee, or individual contributor?
If none of them currently holds a formal role, have they formally left the former Nervos Foundation/CKBA structure?
Regardless of their formal CKBA status, which of the co-founders remain active in the CKB ecosystem, and in what capacity?
This clarification would help the community avoid confusing “not being an execution-team lead” with “having left the project.” Thank you.

recent_posts.content_text:
Aug 8 Updates 2:
Redesigned UI: a single bilingual transcript (speaker + time in the margin, original above, translation below), light/dark themes, per-viewer language view and font sizes with a presentation mode.
image1920×1493 348 KB
Draft-first pipeline: the live draft is promoted to the caption the moment a sentence ends, then silently replaced by a context-aware refined pass.
Rate-limit elimination: diagnosed Volcano’s QPM throttling (misreported as HTTP 500), rebudgeted all quota to the live draft, added classified backoff and quiet backfill — no more failed-translation lines.
Cheaper refined translations (doubao-seed mini).
Robustness: mishearing markers for language-misidentified sentences, reasoning-leak guard, slow-viewer auto-reconnect.
Live demo (no setup): CKB mBabel · Live Demo
